theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: A machine operator reports a fault. What should you do first?
options: Start replacing parts one by one until the machine works
Reset every breaker in the panel to see what happens
Ask what happened and what they saw, heard or smelled
Tell the operator to try running the machine again

questions.stem: Why look at a machine's fault history before you start fault-finding?
options: The fault may have happened before, with a known cause
To find out who used the machine last and then blame them
To see how much the machine cost when it was new
To count how many pages the history file has

questions.stem: Which document helps most when you follow a circuit to find a fault?
options: The supplier's price list for the spare parts
The maker's sales brochure
The Centre's cleaning schedule
The circuit drawings for that equipment

questions.stem: Before you start fault-finding, what should you check about your test instruments?
options: That they are the most costly ones in the store
That they work, are undamaged and are in date
That they have been used on this machine before
That their cases are clean and look like new

questions.stem: Why should you tell the supervisor and the users before isolating a circuit to find a fault?
options: So they can leave early for the rest of the day
So they know the supply will be off and stay safe
So they can stand and watch you and learn how to do it
So they can choose which breaker you switch off

questions.stem: At Level 2, how should fault-finding tests on a circuit be done?
options: With the circuit on, so the fault can be seen
With the circuit on, but wearing rubber gloves
With the breaker off, but with no lock fitted
Isolated, locked off and proved dead

questions.stem: Your voltage tester must be checked on a known live source:
options: before and after you prove the circuit dead
only once a year, when it is sent to be calibrated
only after you have finished the repair
only if the tester has been dropped

questions.stem: A 16 A breaker on a circuit keeps tripping. Someone suggests fitting a 32 A breaker instead. Why is this wrong?
options: A 32 A breaker costs far too much for a small job
A 32 A breaker would trip even more often than before
The cable could overheat before the breaker trips
A 32 A breaker will not fit in the board

questions.stem: Why must a protective device never be bypassed or bridged out?
options: The circuit would have no protection against faults
The circuit would use a lot more electricity each month
The lights on the circuit would flicker
The board would make a humming noise

questions.stem: A breaker has tripped. What should be done before it is reset?
options: Tape the handle so that it cannot trip again
Fit a bigger breaker in its place straight away
Reset it several times until it stays on
Find and put right the cause of the trip

questions.stem: During a repair, you must leave the panel to go for lunch. What should you do?
options: Remove your lock so that others can use the circuit
Leave your lock and tag on, and secure the area
Switch the supply back on until you return
Ask a trainee to stand by the isolator for you

questions.stem: A resistance test from one end of a conductor to the other gives a very high (open circuit) reading. What does this show?
options: The conductor is in good condition
The conductor is touching the earth
There is a break in the conductor
The conductor is a larger size than needed

questions.stem: A breaker tripped, and when the supervisor reset it once, it tripped again at once. Which fault is most likely?
options: An overload that builds up slowly over hours
A short circuit between conductors
A lamp that has reached the end of its life
A loose cover screw on a switch plate

questions.stem: A motor runs for about 30 minutes and then its protection trips. The cable and motor show no damage. What is the most likely fault?
options: A dead short between the line and the neutral
A broken conductor in the motor's supply cable
A lamp that has failed somewhere on the circuit
The motor is drawing too much current

questions.stem: An RCD trips each time one particular appliance is plugged in. What is the most likely fault?
options: Current is leaking to earth from the appliance
The appliance is far too small for the socket it uses
The RCD is set to too high a current
The socket outlet has been fitted upside down

questions.stem: A terminal in a socket outlet is brown and burnt-looking. What is the most likely cause?
options: The socket has been painted with the wrong paint
The cable is a much bigger size than it needs to be
A loose connection has been overheating
The socket was fitted too high on the wall

questions.stem: An insulation resistance test between line and earth gives a very low reading. What does this show?
options: The insulation is in very good condition
The tester's battery is fully charged
The circuit can be switched on safely
The insulation is damaged, wet or faulty

questions.stem: A single-phase motor hums but will not start. Which part is a common cause?
options: The paint on the motor's body
A faulty start or run capacitor
The size of the motor's nameplate
The colour of the cable sheath

questions.stem: A contactor coil shows an open circuit on a resistance test. What does this mean?
options: The coil winding is broken and must be replaced
The coil is in good condition and working well
The coil just needs to be cleaned with a dry cloth
The coil is the wrong colour for the contactor

questions.stem: What is the first step in a logical fault-finding method?
options: Replace the part that fails most often
Switch the supply on and off several times
Find out about the fault and its symptoms
Order new parts so they are ready in time

questions.stem: A lamp does not light. Which checks should come first?
options: Rewire the whole circuit with new cable at once
Change the light fitting for a new one straight away
Replace the distribution board with a new one
Simple ones: the lamp, the switch and the breaker

questions.stem: Why should you change only one thing at a time when fault-finding?
options: So you know which change cured the fault
So the job takes longer and earns more pay
So fewer tools are needed for each step
So the supervisor can rest between changes

questions.stem: Why should you confirm the cause of a fault before you replace parts?
options: So that you can use up the spare parts in the store
So the real fault is fixed, not good parts
So that the machine is kept out of use for longer
So that the old parts can be sold on as scrap

questions.stem: Why should you mark wires before you disconnect them from a device?
options: So they look neat when the cover is put back
So they can carry more current after the repair
So they can be put back on the right terminals
So the next trainee knows you did the job

questions.stem: How can a circuit drawing help when a motor will not start?
options: It shows how much the motor cost when it was new
It shows which trainee wired the motor last time
It shows the colour of the motor's paint and cover
It shows each part in order, so each can be tested

questions.stem: Two identical circuits are side by side; one works and one does not. How can this help you?
options: You can take the parts from the good one and sell them
The good one shows what the faulty one should read
You can join them together so both will work
You can switch off the good one to save power

questions.stem: Which test is used to find a break in a conductor?
options: A continuity test
A polarity test
A power factor test
A frequency test

questions.stem: How should a good single-pole switch, removed from the circuit, read on a continuity test?
options: Open circuit when ON and near 0 Ω when OFF
Near 0 Ω in both the ON and the OFF positions
Near 0 Ω when ON and open circuit when OFF
Open circuit in both the ON and OFF positions

questions.stem: The three windings of a three-phase motor are tested for resistance. Two read 4 Ω and one reads open circuit. What does this show?
options: All three windings are in good condition
The motor is the wrong size for the job it does
The two windings that read 4 Ω are faulty
The winding that reads open circuit is broken

questions.stem: Before an insulation resistance test on a circuit, what must be disconnected?
options: Electronic devices the test voltage could damage
The earth conductor at the main earthing terminal
Every cable clip that holds the circuit in place
The labels on the front of the distribution board

questions.stem: After an insulation resistance test on a long cable, why may the cable need to be discharged?
options: So that the cable cools down after the test
It can hold a charge from the test voltage
So that the tester can be switched off safely
So that the reading on the tester is saved

questions.stem: Why should you touch your meter's leads together before a resistance test?
options: To clean the tips of the probes before use
To warm up the meter's battery for the test
To check that the meter is set to volts
To check the leads and meter read near zero

questions.stem: A continuity test on a protective (earth) conductor gives a high reading. What does this suggest?
options: The earth conductor is in very good condition
The earth conductor is far larger than needed
There is a loose or broken earth connection
The circuit can now be switched on safely

questions.stem: Why must a capacitor be discharged before it is tested or replaced?
options: It can hold a charge that can give you a shock
It will rust if it is left charged for too long
It can only be tested when it is fully warm
It will lose its rating if it stays charged

questions.stem: When replacing a faulty circuit breaker, what must the new one be?
options: A bigger rating, so that it trips less often
The same type and rating as the drawing shows
Any breaker that fits in the space in the board
The cheapest breaker the supplier has in stock

questions.stem: How should a damaged length of cable be repaired?
options: Wrap the damaged part with several layers of tape
Twist the conductors together and push them into the wall
Cover the damage with plaster so nobody can touch it
Replace it, joining only in an approved, reachable box

questions.stem: Why is wrapping cut cable insulation in insulating tape not a proper repair?
options: Tape is too costly to use on a cable repair
Tape makes the cable much too stiff to bend
Tape can work loose and does not protect it
Tape is the wrong colour for the cable sheath

questions.stem: How tight should a terminal screw be after a repair?
options: Tightened to the torque the maker gives
As tight as you can turn it with pliers
Just finger-tight, so it is easy to undo
Loose, so the wire can move as it warms up

questions.stem: A machine's supply cable was damaged by a forklift. After replacing it, what else should be done?
options: Paint the new cable so that it matches the wall colour
Protect the new cable so that it is not hit again
Ask the forklift driver to drive more slowly
Leave some spare cable coiled on the floor

questions.stem: After a repair inside a panel, what must be checked before the cover goes back on?
options: That the panel door has been oiled and cleaned
That the labels on the breakers are all facing up
That the panel is warm enough to switch on
That no tools or offcuts are left inside

questions.stem: After a repair, what must be done before the circuit is handed back?
options: Paint over the repair so that it cannot be seen
Hand it back at once, as the fault has gone
Test it again to show that it is safe and works
Leave a note for the next shift to test it

questions.stem: Who should switch the supply back on after a repair?
options: An authorised person, after the tests have passed
Any worker who is passing the distribution board
The machine operator, as soon as the cover is on
The person who reported the fault in the first place

questions.stem: The repaired circuit works, but the same fault comes back the next day. What does this suggest?
options: The test meter used for the repair was too new
The operator did not say thank you for the repair
The real cause of the fault was not found
The circuit needs a much larger breaker fitted

questions.stem: What should a fault report include?
options: Only the time that you started the job
The fault, its cause, the repair and the tests
The names of everyone who was in the workshop
Your opinion of the machine's operator

questions.stem: You found a fault that you could not repair today. What should you do?
options: Say nothing, so that you are not blamed for it
Leave it switched on so the operator can use it
Fix it quickly with tape and come back next week
Make it safe, tag it and report it for repair

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What is the name of the fault-finding method where you test at the middle of a circuit, then at the middle of the faulty half, and so on?
What is the word for a fault that comes and goes, so the equipment sometimes works and sometimes does not?
A fuse is removed and tested for continuity. The meter reads close to 0 Ω. Is the fuse good or blown?
What is the name of the drawing that shows how each wire is connected, terminal to terminal?
What hand tool is used to remove insulation from the end of a conductor without cutting the strands?
A heater draws 10 A from a 220 V supply. Using V = I × R, what is its resistance in ohms?
What do the letters MCB stand for?
What is the name of the small battery-powered device that gives a known voltage for checking a voltage tester?
When a fuse blows, what is the name of the part inside it that melts?
What do the letters GFCI stand for?
What tool, held against a wall, helps you find the route of a hidden cable?
What is the name of the card or file that keeps the record of every fault and repair on one machine?
A 1 100 W kettle runs on a 220 V supply. Using P = V × I, what current does it draw, in amps?
Before an insulation resistance test on a lighting circuit, what should be taken out of the lamp holders?
What is the name of the device used to join conductors inside a junction box, with a screw, spring or lever?

essays.stem: Describe a logical, step-by-step method for finding a fault in an electrical circuit.
essays.modelAnswer: First I collect information: I ask the operator what happened, when, and what they saw, heard or smelled, and I check the fault history. I look at the symptoms myself, without touching anything, and I check simple things first, such as whether a breaker has tripped or a lamp has failed. I study the drawings to understand how the circuit should work and decide which parts could cause this symptom. I isolate the circuit: switch off, lock off and tag, then prove dead with a tester checked on a known live source before and after. Then I test the likely parts in a sensible order, using continuity, resistance and insulation resistance tests, starting with the most likely and the easiest to reach, or testing at the middle of the circuit to halve the search. I change only one thing at a time. When I find the faulty part, I find out why it failed, repair it, test again, and record the fault, the cause and the repair.
markingPoints: Collects information from the operator and the fault history
Observes the symptoms and checks simple things first
Uses the drawings to work out the likely causes
Isolates and proves dead (tester checked before and after) before testing
Tests in a sensible order, one change at a time; finds the cause, repairs, retests and records

essays.stem: Explain how to safely isolate a circuit before you begin fault-finding on it, and say why each step is needed.
essays.modelAnswer: I tell the supervisor and the users that the circuit will be switched off, so that nobody is surprised or put at risk. I identify the right circuit from the drawings and the board's labels. I switch off the correct breaker or isolator, so that the supply is cut. I lock it off with my own personal padlock, so that nobody can switch it back on, and I fit a tag with my name, the date and the reason, so others know why it is off. Then I prove the circuit dead, because the label may be wrong or there may be another supply. I check my approved two-pole voltage tester on a known live source or proving unit to show that it works, test between all the conductors at the point of work, and then check the tester again to show that it did not fail during the test. Only when the circuit is proved dead do I start testing and repairing. I keep my lock on until the work is finished and tested.
markingPoints: Tells the supervisor and users, and identifies the correct circuit
Switches off the correct device to cut the supply
Locks off with own lock and fits a completed tag, so nobody can switch on
Proves dead at the point of work, because labels can be wrong or there may be another supply
Checks the tester before and after, to show it did not fail; keeps the lock on until finished

essays.stem: Explain the difference between an open circuit, a short circuit and an earth fault. For each one, say how it usually shows itself and how you would test for it.
essays.modelAnswer: An open circuit is a break in the path, for example a broken conductor, a loose terminal or a failed lamp. Current cannot flow, so the equipment does not work, but the protection does not usually trip. With the circuit isolated, a continuity test along the conductor shows a very high (open circuit) reading where the break is. A short circuit is where the line conductor touches the neutral, or another line, with almost no resistance between them. A very large current flows, so the fuse blows or the breaker trips at once, often with a bang or burn marks. With the loads disconnected, a resistance or insulation resistance test between the conductors gives a reading close to zero. An earth fault is where a live conductor touches earth or an earthed metal part. Current leaks to earth, so an RCD or GFCI trips, or a fuse blows if the fault is large. An insulation resistance test between the live conductors and earth gives a low reading.
markingPoints: Open circuit: a break; equipment does not work, protection does not usually trip
Open circuit found by a continuity test (very high reading at the break)
Short circuit: line touches neutral or another line; trips or blows at once
Short circuit found by a resistance or insulation test between conductors (near zero), loads disconnected
Earth fault: live touches earth; RCD trips; insulation test to earth gives a low reading

essays.stem: Describe how you would use continuity tests to find a break in a lighting circuit that has one switch and three lamps.
essays.modelAnswer: First I isolate the lighting circuit: switch off, lock off and tag, then prove dead with a tester checked on a known live source before and after. I remove the lamps so that they do not affect the readings, and I look at the drawing to see the route of the line, the switch wire and the neutral. I set my meter to continuity and touch the leads together to check that it reads near zero. I can use a long test lead, or link two conductors at the far end, to test each conductor from the board to each lamp position. I test the line from the breaker to the switch, then across the switch in the ON and OFF positions, then the switch wire to each lamp holder, and the neutral from each lamp holder back to the neutral bar. A good conductor reads near zero; a break gives an open circuit reading. When one section reads open, I test smaller parts of that section and look closely at its joints and terminals until I find the break. Then I repair it and test again.
markingPoints: Isolates and proves dead with a tester checked before and after
Removes the lamps and uses the drawing to see the route of each conductor
Sets the meter and does a lead check
Tests each section in order: line to switch, the switch, switch wire to lamps, neutral back
Narrows down the section that reads open, finds the break, repairs it and retests

essays.stem: Explain why a fuse or circuit breaker must never be replaced with one of a higher rating, and must never be bypassed, even if it keeps tripping.
essays.modelAnswer: A fuse or breaker is chosen to protect the cable and the equipment on that circuit. Its rating is matched to the current that the cable can safely carry. If it keeps tripping, it is doing its job: it is telling us that there is a fault or an overload. If a higher rating is fitted, a fault or overload could let more current flow than the cable can carry, without the device tripping. The cable would overheat, its insulation could melt, and this can cause a fire or an electric shock. Bypassing the device, for example with a piece of wire, removes the protection altogether, so a short circuit could cause a fire, damage the board or cause serious injury. The right action is to isolate the circuit, find the cause of the trips, such as a damaged cable, a faulty appliance or too much load on one circuit, and put it right. The protective device is only replaced with one of the same type and rating as the design shows.
markingPoints: The rating is matched to what the cable can safely carry
Tripping is a warning of a fault or overload
A higher rating lets the cable overheat: fire or shock
Bypassing removes all protection
Correct action: isolate, find and fix the cause; replace only with the same type and rating

essays.stem: Describe how to carry out an insulation resistance test on a cable or a motor safely, and explain what the results mean.
essays.modelAnswer: I isolate the circuit or motor: switch off, lock off and tag, then prove dead with a tester checked on a known live source before and after. I disconnect or remove anything that could be damaged by the test voltage or would affect the reading, such as electronic devices, drives, dimmers, surge protectors and lamps. I warn people nearby and make sure nobody can touch the conductors during the test, because the tester applies a high DC voltage. I check the tester and its leads, and choose the test voltage that the code or the maker gives for that circuit. I test between the live conductors, and between each live conductor and earth; for a motor, I test each winding to the frame. A high reading, in megohms, means the insulation is good. A low reading means the insulation is damaged, dirty or wet, and the fault must be found before the circuit is used. After the test I let the tester discharge the cable, then reconnect everything and record the results.
markingPoints: Isolates and proves dead with a tester checked before and after
Disconnects electronics, lamps and anything the test could damage or upset
Warns others, because a high DC test voltage is used; uses the right test voltage
Tests between conductors and to earth (motor windings to frame)
High reading good, low reading a fault; discharges, reconnects and records

essays.stem: Explain how you would properly repair a damaged cable, and a burnt, loose connection in a socket outlet.
essays.modelAnswer: First the circuit is isolated, locked off, tagged and proved dead with a tester checked before and after. For the damaged cable, I find out what damaged it, such as a sharp edge, rats, heat or a vehicle. Where possible I replace the whole length. If joints are allowed, I cut out the damaged part and join in new cable of the same type and size, using approved connectors inside a suitable junction box that can be reached later. I never just wrap the damage in tape. I protect the new cable so that it is not damaged again. For the burnt socket outlet, I check how far the heat damage goes. A burnt outlet must be replaced, and if the conductor ends are blackened or hardened, I cut them back to clean copper. I strip the right length, fit the conductors fully into the terminals and tighten them to the maker's torque. Then I test the repair and record what I found and what I did.
markingPoints: Isolates and proves dead first
Finds the cause of the cable damage and protects the new cable
Replaces the length, or joins with approved connectors in a reachable box; never just tape
Replaces the burnt outlet and cuts conductors back to clean copper
Correct strip length, terminals tightened to torque; tests and records

essays.stem: Describe the tests and checks you would carry out after a repair, before the circuit is handed back for use.
essays.modelAnswer: Before anything is switched on, I check that the repair is complete: every terminal is tight, no bare conductors show, covers are fitted and no tools or offcuts are left inside. With the circuit still isolated, I do the dead tests. I test the continuity of the protective (earth) conductor, to make sure every metal part is earthed. I test the continuity of the circuit conductors I worked on. I do an insulation resistance test, with electronics and lamps disconnected, to make sure there is no short circuit or earth fault. I check polarity, so that switches and fuses are in the line conductor. I compare the results with the expected values and record them. Then I remove my lock and tag, and an authorised person switches on and does any live checks the code requires, such as RCD tests. Finally a functional check shows that the equipment works as it should and that the original fault has gone, and I explain the repair to the user.
markingPoints: Visual and mechanical check: tight terminals, no bare conductors, covers on, nothing left inside
Earth continuity and circuit continuity tests
Insulation resistance (electronics and lamps out) and polarity
Results compared and recorded; lock removed; an authorised person switches on and does live checks
Functional check that the fault has gone; user told about the repair

essays.stem: Describe what should be written in a fault report, and explain why good records of faults and repairs are important.
essays.modelAnswer: A fault report should give the date and time, the equipment and its location, and who reported the fault. It describes the fault as it was reported and the symptoms I found. It lists the tests I did and their results, the cause of the fault, and what I did to repair it, including the parts used, their ratings and any part numbers. It gives the tests done after the repair and their results, how long the job took, and whether anything still needs to be done, such as a part on order. I sign and date it, and the supervisor checks it. Good records are important because they show that the work was done safely and properly. They help the next person who works on the equipment, because a fault that keeps coming back can be seen in the history and its real cause found. They help plan maintenance and order spare parts, and they can be shown to an inspector or the client.
markingPoints: Date, equipment, location, who reported it, and the symptoms
Tests done and results, and the cause found
Repair done and the parts used, with ratings
Tests after repair, time taken, anything outstanding; signed and checked
Why: proof of safe work, history shows repeat faults, helps planning and spares

essays.stem: A motor controlled by a direct-on-line (DOL) starter will not start when the start button is pressed. Describe how you would find the fault using dead tests on the control circuit.
essays.modelAnswer: I ask the operator what happened and check simple things first, such as whether the overload relay has tripped or the control fuse has blown. I study the control circuit drawing. Then I isolate the starter: switch off, lock off and tag, then prove dead with a tester checked on a known live source before and after, including the control supply if it comes from somewhere else. I mark any wires I need to disconnect. With my meter on continuity, I test each part of the control circuit in turn, following the drawing: the control fuse, the overload relay's contact, the stop button (closed when not pressed), the start button (closed only when pressed), and the wiring between them. Then I test the contactor coil's resistance: a reading near the expected value is good, while an open circuit reading means the coil is broken. A part that reads open when it should be closed is the fault. I find out why it failed, replace it with the same type and rating, retest, and record it.
markingPoints: Gets information, checks the overload and control fuse first, uses the drawing
Isolates the starter and any separate control supply, and proves dead
Tests the control parts in turn: fuse, overload contact, stop (closed), start (closes when pressed), wiring
Tests the coil resistance and interprets the result
Replaces the faulty part like-for-like, retests and records

practical1.title: Find and repair faults on a lighting circuit training board
practical1.brief: The instructor sets up a lighting circuit on a training board (for example two lamps on a one-way switch and one lamp on two-way switching, fed from a breaker), and puts in at least one fault for each member of the group (four or five faults) while the group is out of the room, such as an open circuit in a switch wire, a loose terminal, a wrong connection at a switch, a broken wire between the two-way switches and a failed lamp. The instructor shows the group the symptoms by operating the switches, then switches the board off. The group then: (1) writes down the symptoms and studies the drawing; (2) isolates the board, locks off, tags and proves dead with a tester checked on a proving unit before and after; (3) uses continuity and resistance tests to find each fault, writing every test and reading on the fault sheet; (4) repairs each fault properly; (5) does the dead tests again (continuity, insulation resistance with the lamps removed, and polarity); (6) hands the board back to the instructor, who switches on and checks that every lamp now works. Each member finds and repairs at least one fault while the assessor watches, and explains how they found it. If the board cannot take that many faults at once, the instructor sets a fresh fault between members' turns, so that every member has one of their own. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: Lighting circuit training board with faults set by the instructor
The circuit drawing for the board
An approved two-pole voltage tester and a proving unit
A multimeter or continuity tester, and an insulation resistance tester
Personal padlocks, tags and a hasp
Screwdrivers, wire strippers, side cutters, spare cable, connectors and spare lamps
Fault-finding sheet and test record sheet
photos: The symptoms written down beside the drawing
The board locked off and tagged, and the tester being checked on the proving unit
A member proving dead at the board
Each fault found, with the test leads on the faulty part and the reading visible
Each repair, close up, before the cover is refitted
The dead tests after repair, and the completed test record
The board working after the instructor switched it on, with the completed fault sheet
checklist: Recorded the symptoms and used the drawing to decide what to test
Isolated, locked off and tagged the board, and proved dead with a tester checked before and after
Used continuity and resistance tests correctly, with a lead check first
Tested in a logical order and recorded each test and reading
Found the fault they were given and explained how they found it
Repaired the fault properly: right materials, tight terminals, no bare copper
Carried out the dead tests after the repair and recorded the results
Left the board tidy and handed it back for the instructor to switch on
safety: Never work live: all testing and repair is done with the board isolated, locked off and proved dead
Only the instructor switches the board on, to show the symptoms and for the final check
Check the voltage tester on the proving unit before and after proving dead
Warn others and keep hands off the board during insulation resistance tests
Wear safety glasses when cutting and stripping cable
Follow the Centre's rules for the training boards

practical2.title: Find and repair faults on a motor starter control circuit
practical2.brief: The instructor sets up a DOL starter controlling a small motor on a training board, and puts in one fault for each member of the group (four or five faults), such as an open circuit in the stop button wiring, a missing link to the hold-in contact, a loose wire on the overload relay contact and a broken wire to the coil. The instructor shows the group the symptoms (for example, the motor does not start, or runs only while start is held in), then switches off. The group then: (1) writes down the symptoms and studies the control and power drawings; (2) isolates the starter and any separate control supply, locks off, tags and proves dead with a tester checked on a proving unit before and after; (3) uses continuity and resistance tests on the control circuit, following the drawing, to find each fault, recording each test and reading; (4) tests the contactor coil's resistance and the motor windings (each winding's resistance, and each winding to the frame with the insulation resistance tester); (5) repairs each fault, marking any wires before they are moved; (6) repeats the dead tests and fills in a fault report; (7) hands back to the instructor, who switches on and runs a functional test (start, hold in, stop, overload). Each member finds and repairs at least one fault and explains it to the assessor. If the board cannot take that many faults at once, the instructor sets a fresh fault between members' turns, so that every member has one of their own. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: DOL starter and small motor on a training board, with faults set by the instructor
Power and control circuit drawings for the starter
An approved two-pole voltage tester and a proving unit

checklist: Recorded the symptoms and used the drawings to decide what to test
Isolated the starter and any separate control supply, locked off, tagged and proved dead with a tester checked before and after
Tested the control circuit parts in a logical order and recorded each reading
Read the results correctly (closed contacts near 0 Ω; open contacts and breaks open circuit)
Tested the coil and the motor windings correctly and explained the results
Marked wires before moving them, and repaired faults with the right materials and markers
Repeated the dead tests and filled in the fault report fully
Explained their fault, its cause and the repair to the assessor
safety: Never work live: all testing and repair is done isolated, locked off and proved dead
Isolate any separate control supply as well as the main supply
Only the instructor switches on, to show the symptoms and for the final functional test
Keep clear of the motor shaft during the functional test
Warn others and keep hands off during insulation resistance tests
Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules
